body_markdown:
About two years ago (the summer after I purchased my troublesome regret-buying-it-but-it-made-sense-at-the-time 2008 Nissan Armada), while resurrecting the SUV’s air conditioning, I had to deal with the woodpecker-under-the-dash issue of a bad HVAC actuator. If you don’t know, the actuator is a little cigarette-pack-sized box containing a little electric motor and a few gears. When it’s sent a signal, it opens and closes a flap or moves a blend door. When the gears inside the actuator strip their teeth or some other bit of plastic breaks but the motor continues turning, you hear the aforementioned woodpecker-like rapping noise. This is an extremely common problem in Armadas, Titans, and corresponding Infiniti models.[In this first go-round](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/the-hack-mechanic/trying-to-get-my-a-c-system-through-the-summer-part-ii/) , the problem actually wasn’t in the actuator but in the rotating plate that it’s attached to.


Pulling the actuator on the right side of the heater box was relatively easy. It was removing and replacing the plate that moves the lever that moves a certain blend door that was difficult.


Rob Siegel


Then, last winter, I was confronted with another head of the actuator hydra, this one on the left side of the heater box that did the all-important winter job of opening up the flow of air to the footwells. In order to figure out which part I needed to order, I delved into what I referred to as[the Actuator Rosetta Stone](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/the-hack-mechanic/decoding-the-nissan-armada-actuator-rosetta-stone/) and decoded it. Because the broken part was so easy to access and replace, I spent $22 on Amazon for that well-known high-quality brand “A-Premium” (that was sufficiently sarcastic, right?) even though 11% of the reviews are one-star and say things like “broke in a few months.”


The two different kinds of actuators on the Armada. The “innie” on the left directly moves a door. The “outie” on the right moves a lever or a plate (or both) that moves a door.


Nissan


As I wrote a few weeks ago, I sold my 1999 BMW M Coupe (a.k.a. the “clown shoe”), making it the fourth car I’ve sold in the past year, cutting the tally down from 14 to 10. A few people commented that they were surprised that I hadn’t (or haven’t) sold the Armada, since I rarely use it and all I do is complain about it. In the piece about[foolishly passing on a well-priced unicorn BMW wagon](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/the-hack-mechanic/semi-stalking-yet-another-bmw-unicorn/) (and no, I never heard back from the seller), I mentioned that I initially considered going up there with the Armada towing a U-Haul trailer to buy and grab the car, but it was during a hot stretch in August, and the Armada’s air conditioning wasn’t working due to a refrigerant leak. I then spent an hour looking for the leak, couldn’t find it (the Armada has a complex A/C system with lines that run under it to the rear air), and I noted that, if I sell it, fall would be a good time, as working A/C falls off as a must-have. However, while I was poking around in the Armada, I was greeted by the dreaded woodpecker sound coming not only from the front but also the back.


So when the first crack of cool autumn air rolled in in early September, I gave the Armada and its rapping sound a look, with an eye toward making the heat, at least, fully functional for a fall sale. These actuators don’t seem to remember their positions, so they go through a cycle of rotating to establish baselines even if you don’t change the heater settings (maybe it’s because I have a disconnect switch on the battery so it doesn’t run down during its long sits), so when you turn the key, they all begin hunting, and if they’re broken, they let you know with the loud characteristic *rap-rap-rap* . I hunted around with my ears and hands and determined that the noise from the front was coming from the same left-of-console actuator I’d replaced last winter. *Gee, I guess those one-star reviews were right on the money.* At least I knew this one was easy to replace.


But the noise from the back of the car was almost certainly coming from the air/heat blend door actuator in the rear climate control box, and unfortunately, it’s behind a cover that’s three feet long. I tried to localize the sound further with my ears and hands to see where in that three-foot expanse it was, and had a surprising amount of trouble doing so.


The woodpecker—I mean, actuator—was somewhere behind this.


Rob Siegel


I looked online and found that, according to several videos, to get at the actuator, you need to pull off that long cover, and to do that, you need to remove quite a few things. I was surprised to find there was a pop-off access panel for the expansion valve in the cover, but not one for the much more failure-prone actuator. Had I found a video that showed where to go full Hack on the cover and slice it open with a hot knife, I gladly would’ve done so, but I didn’t, so I had no alternative but to pull it apart.


Why there’s this access panel for the expansion valve but not one for the actuator is beyond me.


Rob Siegel


Like many things you dread, it actually wasn’t bad at all. I found a video that showed that you don’t even need to pull the entire panel completely off—there’s plenty of room to access the actuator if the front of the panel remains attached near the middle seat. Pull up the rear cargo floor, undo the little panel with the cargo tie-down points on it, disconnect the rear right belt anchor, use a pry tool to pull up the cover, give it a good yank to unsnap about two feet of snap fasteners, undo the electrical connectors to the rear cigarette lighter socket and to the fold-down third-row seats, and just muscle the thing to the left far enough to get your arm in there to undo the electrical connector to the actuator and unscrew the three 5.5mm fasteners holding it in. I think that, end-to-end, I had it out in less than 20 minutes.


The actuator is in that yellow area.


Rob Siegel


Once I pulled it out, I could see what I needed to know to replace it (if it was bad), which was that it was an “outie” actuator. However, when I tested it in place, it spun and didn’t make any noise. I pulled the cover off it, watched it in motion, and there didn’t appear to be anything wrong with it.


Watching the actuator in, uh, action.


Rob Siegel


However, when I pulled it apart, I could see that one of the gears was badly stripped.


It’s hard to see, but most of the vertical splines on the camera-facing side of the gear are missing.


Rob Siegel


Knowing that the thing was indeed bad, I sourced a replacement. The price to replace it with a genuine Nissan OE part was almost $90 via eBay. Because accessing it was much easier than I expected, for better or worse (well, clearly worse), I went with an inexpensive aftermarket part. Hopefully I’ll have better luck with it than I had with the cheap footwell actuator that only lasted a few months.


And speaking of said footwell actuator, the price of the OE part was about $60. But because it’s so easy to replace, I again went with the aftermarket option, though this time I selected a Four Seasons part with much better reviews than the, ahem, A-Premium part. I had it changed in five minutes.


Done.


Rob Siegel


So, for about fifty bucks, I shut off the woodpecker surround-sound system, made the heat functional for fall/winter, and fixed something so I won’t have to apologize about it if and when I sell it. We’ll see if my thrifty choices were smart or idiotic. If I don’t find a car that I need to buy and tow back home in the next few months, I think I’ll let the Armada go for whatever someone wants to pay me for it, which will likely be less than half what I have in it. Yes, I need to own needy cars in order to generate all this weekly content, but while I may have gotten nearly a dozen articles out of the electric A/C in the ’69 Lotus Elan +2, four articles on the Armada exhaust and three pieces on actuators is probably a good place to stop!


***
